did_you_know.text: Did you know? This verse contains rhetorical questions about the one who ascended to heaven, gathered the wind, wrapped up the waters, and established the earth. At the end, it also asks what his name is and what his son’s name is.
Did you know? Proverbs 30 describes every word of God as flawless—purified and refined—and presents God as a shield to those who take refuge in him.
Did you know? Agur makes two requests before he dies, which he states in the following verse: to be kept from lies and falsehood, and to live without extreme poverty or excessive wealth.
Did you know? The speaker explains why he asks for financial balance: abundance might lead him to deny God, while extreme poverty might lead him to steal and dishonor God’s name.
Did you know? The image of the leech describes two daughters crying, “Give! Give!”—that is, demanding more and more. It is followed by a list of things that are never satisfied.

Did you know? This passage presents four wonderful things whose paths are difficult to trace: the way of an eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, a ship in the middle of the sea, and a man with a young woman.

Did you know? Four small creatures are described as exceptionally wise: ants that prepare their food in summer, rock badgers that make their homes in the crags, locusts that move without a king, and geckos that can be found even in kings’ palaces.

Did you know? After describing the small creatures, the chapter presents four creatures with impressive bearing: the lion, the strutting creature—interpreted either as a rooster or a greyhound—the male goat, and a king whom no one can oppose.
Did you know? The chapter ends with practical advice: if someone has acted foolishly out of arrogance or planned something evil, he should put his hand over his mouth and stop speaking harmfully.
Did you know? The final verse uses a vivid comparison: just as churning milk produces butter, anger and pressure can produce bloodshed and strife.
